analysis.investment_thesis: Indigo Paints is a differentiated challenger brand in Indian decorative paints with a clean balance sheet and expanding OCF, but a sharp growth deceleration in FY2025 (revenue +2.7%, net profit -4.7% YoY) disqualifies it from Fisher's core criterion of sustained 20%+ compounding. At 26.9x PE on declining earnings, the price already embeds a growth premium the business is currently failing to deliver.
key_strengths: Nearly debt-free balance sheet (D/E: 0.02) with strong OCF acceleration (₹65 Cr → ₹206 Cr over 4 years) — capital discipline is excellent.
High gross margins (45.68%) signal genuine product differentiation (fluorescent, tile, and roof paints) vs. commodity competitors.
Heavy CWIP build (₹221 Cr in FY2025) suggests capacity expansion underway — if monetized, could re-accelerate top-line growth.
key_risks: Growth deceleration is alarming: revenue nearly flat in FY2025 (+2.7%) after 21.7% growth in FY2024 — the single largest Fisher red flag.
Operates in a market dominated by Asian Paints, Berger, and Kansai Nerolac; moat depends on niche differentiation that incumbents can replicate.
ROE at 14.6% is well below Fisher's 20% threshold, and declining net profit (₹149→₹142 Cr) signals margin pressure in a competitive repricing environment.
red_flags: FY2025 revenue growth collapsed to 2.7% — this is not a blip, it follows a massive capex cycle that hasn't translated to volumes yet.
Net profit and EBITDA both declined YoY in FY2025 — earnings momentum has reversed.
Finance costs up 44% CAGR (albeit off a tiny base) as CWIP surged to ₹221 Cr — execution risk on new capacity is real.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From my scuttlebutt perspective, Indigo Paints deserves credit for carving a niche in Indian decorative paints through genuinely differentiated products — its fluorescent and tile-paint categories created pull with painters and applicators where legacy giants were complacent. The balance sheet is exemplary: virtually zero debt, four consecutive years of positive OCF, and growing reserves (₹1,019 Cr in FY2025). These are signs of honest, capital-conscious management. The promoter holding at 53.88% and strong DII backing (21.13%) suggest institutional confidence in long-term fundamentals.

However, the FY2025 numbers give me serious pause. Revenue grew only ₹35 Cr on a ₹1,306 Cr base — barely 2.7%. Net profit fell. EBITDA fell. This is the year the company was supposed to be harvesting its heavy FY2022-23 capex cycle (₹199 Cr capex, ₹251 Cr CWIP in FY2023). The new CWIP of ₹221 Cr in FY2025 means another heavy spend cycle is beginning before the last one proved its returns. I require companies in my portfolio to demonstrate they can grow sales and profits year after year — Indigo Paints has interrupted that record. Until the new capacity translates to ≥20% revenue growth resumption, this is a HOLD, not a conviction buy.
